_comment: Hand-authored. Every entry carries exactly one reference, and build_authored.py refuses the
file if any entry lacks one. Seeded from the marker list of the owner's WebXR Milky Way
Atlas ships numbers with no citation and two of them are wrong, both recorded below.
Deliberately SHORT. Named molecular clouds are not listed here: 94 of them ship in
galaxy/namedclouds.json, generated from Zucker et al. 2020 with a measured distance and an
uncertainty each, in this same schema. Five globular landmarks carry no coordinates at all;
they name a row of galaxy/globulars.csgp, so their positions exist once.
Not here, and why: open clusters (Pleiades, Hyades) -- no staged source carries their
distances, and a recalled parallax is exactly the failure this project has paid for before.
Local Group landmarks belong to the `galaxies` lane (ATLAS-PARITY MWA-18b).

places.name: Sun
places.description: You are here. Every position in the Milky Way layer is heliocentric.
places.reference: origin of the heliocentric frame, by definition

places.name: Sgr A*
places.description: The 4.3-million-solar-mass black hole at the Galactic Centre. The distance here is GalaxyModel.R0 = 8.15 kpc so that the arm model and the Galactic Centre agree; GRAVITY Collaboration give 8.178 kpc (2019) and 8.277 kpc (2022). The Atlas places it at 8178 pc with no citation.
places.reference: Reid & Brunthaler 2004, ApJ 616, 872 (radio position); R0 = 8.15 +/- 0.15 kpc from Reid et al. 2019, ApJ 885, 131

places.name: Local Bubble
places.description: The supernova-blown cavity the Sun sits inside, about 1000 light years across and peanut-shaped, with every nearby young star forming on its surface. The Atlas gives its size as 150 pc in one place and 100 pc in another; neither is the published figure, which is about 300 pc across.
places.reference: Zucker et al. 2022, Nature 601, 334 (the Local Bubble's surface as the site of nearby star formation; ~1000 ly across)

places.name: Radcliffe Wave
places.description: A 2.7 kpc coherent, oscillating wave of star-forming gas passing about 300 pc from the Sun. Its fitted spine ships as galaxy/radcliffe.csgp; this entry is the label.
places.reference: Alves et al. 2020, Nature 578, 237 (discovery); Konietzka et al. 2024, Nature 628, 62 (the oscillation and the fitted spine)

places.name: Orion complex
places.description: M42, the Horsehead and the Flame: the nearest massive star-forming region.
places.reference: Menten, Reid, Forbrich & Brunthaler 2007, A&A 474, 515 (VLBA parallax to the Orion Nebula Cluster, 414 +/- 7 pc)

places.name: Orion Nebula (M42)
places.description: The blister of ionised gas on the near face of the Orion A cloud, lit by the Trapezium.
places.reference: Menten, Reid, Forbrich & Brunthaler 2007, A&A 474, 515 (VLBA parallax, 414 +/- 7 pc)

places.name: Crab Nebula (M1)
places.description: The remnant of SN 1054 and its pulsar. The pulsar's spin frequency is the one number here that is measured to nine digits; the distance is the one that is worst known.
places.reference: Trimble 1973, PASP 85, 579 (distance ~2 kpc); spin frequency 29.6 Hz at MJD 58058 from Lyne et al. 2018, MNRAS 478, 3832

places.name: 47 Tucanae
places.description: The second-brightest globular cluster, and one of the densest.
places.reference: position and distance from galaxy/globulars.csgp (Local Volume Database v1.1.1); that file carries the per-object distance reference

places.name: Omega Centauri
places.description: The most luminous globular cluster of the Milky Way, and probably the stripped core of a swallowed dwarf galaxy.
places.reference: position and distance from galaxy/globulars.csgp (Local Volume Database v1.1.1)

places.name: M4
places.description: The nearest globular cluster to the Sun.
places.reference: position and distance from galaxy/globulars.csgp (Local Volume Database v1.1.1)

places.name: M13
places.description: The Hercules cluster, target of the 1974 Arecibo message.
places.reference: position and distance from galaxy/globulars.csgp (Local Volume Database v1.1.1)

places.name: M15
places.description: One of the most core-collapsed globulars known.
places.reference: position and distance from galaxy/globulars.csgp (Local Volume Database v1.1.1)
